selectedFirstIdea.rationale: This experiment is direct evidence that even short, generic prompt constraints can change the editorial hierarchy in systematic ways. selectedFirstIdea.title: Candidate prompt change displaced the intended editorial hierarchy and triggered a rollback
selectedFirstIdea.description: A single added section in the Narrative user prompt — intended to “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” — produced consistent, repeatable degradations in both Narrative and Compose outputs: company-level identity and audience were subordinated while orchestration became central, unsupported claims appeared, and the change was not promoted. The production prompt was restored byte-for-byte.
selectedFirstIdea.audience: Prompt engineers, editorial leads, release managers
selectedFirstIdea.rationale: This experiment shows a straightforward operational risk: even a small, generic prompt change can reliably alter high-level emphasis and introduce editorial regressions that fail promotion gates. Teams deciding whether to change system prompts need evidence that a change preserves the intended hierarchy before promoting it.
selectedFirstIdea.evidence: Facts: the candidate prompt added one generic section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” and contained no Nuëyon-specific wording; three candidate Narrative runs scored mean 4.00/10 vs baseline mean 6.00/10; three candidate Compose runs scored mean 3.33/10 vs baseline mean 5.67/10; all candidate Narrative and Compose runs made orchestration central and introduced unsupported additions; decision: “Do not promote. Candidate was worse on mean score… failed the orchestration hierarchy and factual restraint gates in every run,” and production prompt was restored (byte-for-byte SHA match). Inference: the added prompt section correlated with the observed editorial drift and regressions. Unknowns: the exact causal mechanism inside the model that produced the drift (e.g., how the new phrasing interacted with the Synthesis content or model internals).

selectedFirstIdea.title: Narrative is the recurrent first-visible locus of pipeline hierarchy drift
selectedFirstIdea.description: Across the inspected runs, the Narrative stage most frequently shows the earliest observable departure from the requested company-first editorial hierarchy — turning a company introduction into a product/architecture-led story or adding unsupported audience/validation language.
selectedFirstIdea.audience: Content architects, experiment designers, product/content teams operating Nuëyon.Compose pipelines
selectedFirstIdea.rationale: Why it matters: If Narrative is the stage where the intended company-first story most often becomes product- or orchestration-first, then interventions that preserve story priority are likeliest to succeed when targeted at Narrative (prompt constraints, guardrails, checks). Prioritizing Narrative fixes limits rework downstream and focuses experimentation where the problem appears. Gaps and uncertainty: the evidence localizes the first observable shift but does not prove Narrative is the root cause in every run — some runs shift earlier (Idea or Synthesis) and Compose can amplify issues. A controlled trial is needed to confirm causation before large-scale process changes.
selectedFirstIdea.evidence: Explicit observations: Narrative is identified as the earliest visible hierarchy shift in Experiment 007 runs 001–002; Experiment 008 A-002; Experiment 009 baseline 002/003 and candidate runs 001–003. Cross-experiment summary states: “Narrative is the most recurrent first visible hierarchy shift in the available records.” The per-run tables show concrete Narrative-level examples (e.g., turning an orchestration product detail into the through-line, inventing audiences, adding validation framing). The report clarifies this is an observable stage-level pattern, not a demonstrated model causal chain.
